Thomas Tuchel faces a fight to regain the full trust of his England players, despite claiming that “99.9 per cent” of supporters do not talk about the semi-final defeat by Argentina.

Telegraph Sport reported that players were shocked and disappointed by Tuchel’s approach to the final 30 minutes of the World Cup semi-final.

It can now be revealed that doubts linger among England players over Tuchel’s ability to get the best out of his squad and ultimately lead them to glory in the next European Championship.

There is also some lasting unhappiness over Tuchel’s perceived unwillingness to take ultimate responsibility for England’s World Cup exit and his claim that ball possession was not in “the DNA” of the nation’s players.

Sources indicate that tuchel has spoken of fostering a “brotherhood” within the England squad, but a source told Telegraph Sport: “He still has work to do to get all the players fully behind him again. What happened at the World Cup and some of his comments caused some damage that has not just disappeared.”.

Tuchel has no concerns over the commitment of his players and said: “I have no doubt how keen they are. No doubt. I know them, I was seven weeks with them. We had a qualification campaign together, we are 18 months together, I have no doubt that we step up and produce performances in the next cycle. I’m responsible for that.”.

One player who did not travel to the World Cup and is not part of Tuchel’s latest England squad for four Nations League games is Morgan Gibbs-White. His partner, Britney De Villiers, took a swipe at Tuchel by posting an image on Instagram that referenced the fact the Nottingham Forest man is the only Premier League player to have created five or more chances in every match he has played this season.

There is no immediate sign that Tuchel is ready to change his approach, as he refused to accept the country were angered by his tactics and substitutions in the Argentina game.

In an attempt to gloss over the nature of England’s missed opportunity in the United States, Tuchel claimed that the bronze-medal victory over France was “one of the nicest experiences ever” for supporters and that he did not lose any sleep over his World Cup squad selection.

Tuchel’s defence of the World Cup campaign also included the revelation that his Football Association bosses had assured the England head coach that his job was safe before the last-16 victory over Mexico.

“I tell you something, like 99.9 per cent of the fans don’t speak about substitutions, tactical twists,” Tuchel said. “They speak about where they have watched the Mexico game, they speak about the second half, the energy of the Croatia match, they speak about how nerve-wracking it was to watch our match against Congo and where they celebrated.

“This is how it should be, this is what a World Cup is for, to connect with the people and to give them experiences that they will not forget. And this is the feedback that I get.”.

Industry observers note that asked if he had received any negative feedback at all since the World Cup, Tuchel answered: “No. Not at all. Do you think that’s necessary? I had some quite bad stuff between Argentina and France. [But] No [not since I’ve been back in England].”.

The FA publicly backed Tuchel after the defeat by Argentina, but the German has now revealed that he was privately told his job was safe well before that.

It has been revealed that even if England had lost to Mexico and failed to reach the last eight of the World Cup, Tuchel has claimed he would not have been sacked. He said: “There was a moment, a very special moment, before the Mexico game where we had a talk and my bosses told me ‘we know that anything can happen in a football match, we know that anything can happen in a match in Mexico, in a World Cup match, but don’t worry, we see what’s going on and we want to continue like this’.

“It was a beautiful moment for me as a coach. I felt this kind of freedom to take my choices and to just coach freely, and there was never a doubt in my mind that we would continue together and there was obviously never a doubt in their mind.”.

England secured their best World Cup finish since 1966 by winning the bronze-medal game against France in a chaotic match in Miami.

“If you look at the 6-4 against France, people talk about it like it’s one of their nicest experiences ever, to watch a football match,” Tuchel remarked. “So maybe I have to compromise in my wish for control, for a little bit more chaos, embrace the chaos, and maybe it brings out the best.”.

Tuchel has named his first England squad since the World Cup for four Nations League games against Spain, Czech Republic (home and away) and Croatia. He has recalled Cole Palmer and Trent Alexander-Arnold to his squad, but insists he has lost no sleep over not taking the pair to the World Cup.

Industry observers note that “I was very happy with the [World Cup] squad selection, we put a lot of effort and emphasis into the squad selection,” Tuchel said. “And I had a lot of sleepless nights, but I had not one sleepless night about our selection, because I was more than seven weeks with this group of players, and they were nothing but fantastic. I think the spirit that we built and the mentality that we highlighted brought us to the place that we got.

Recent findings suggest that “It feels unfulfilled, but, yeah, that’s how it is. We need to move forward with the decisions in the Argentina game. And sometimes as a coach, you can only win if you win. So now we know the result, and we didn’t win. Of course, I reflect and, of course, I’m very critical of myself. But the question that is also still lingering around is, who knows what would have happened? Who knows if we hadn’t made any substitutions what would have happened? And would we have the same sleepless nights?

“So, there’s not much sense in torturing ourselves, looking back. It’s moving forward, but the team, like I said, did brilliantly. And I will not allow 30 minutes against Argentina to override how we view this World Cup.”.

Industry observers note that tuchel had warnings for Palmer and Alexander-Arnold, as he noted: “It is one thing to be nominated, by the way, with Cole and getting your ticket back in the squad, but it’s another thing to play and keep your place. It’s about when he comes and he needs to show these kinds of performances.”.

Sources indicate that on Alexander-Arnold, Tuchel added: “Now it’s time to fight for his place. He always noted he’s up for a fight, especially for England. So it’s a need to prove that.”.

Recent findings suggest that tuchel noted that Alexander-Arnold has been called up as a right-back, rather than a midfielder. Asked if the Real Madrid player offers enough defensively, he answered by saying: “He has to, he has to. It’s necessary. My conviction is that he will, but he has no choice.”.

Tuchel has now finished his broadcast duties. It was quite a strange performance from him. I don’t recall ever seeing him read from notes before. His little joke about his bosses telling him off was awkward and felt rehearsed, and the stuff about 99.9 per cent of England fans talking about Mexico and the second half against Croatia was delusional.

Sources indicate that it was also jarring to hear him claim that the FA had basically assured Tuchel that his job was safe straight after England beat Mexico. It was a special night, undoubtedly, but did it really deserve that sort of reaction?

Industry observers note that “I wanted to give Jarrad a chance. It was a 51 per cent decision on Jarrad.

“I don’t have a clear picture on what he is all about and have a very clear picture on what Levi can bring us.”.

“It makes no sense to nominate three, four, five number 10s. It just does not help anyone. We can see the form that Morgan [Gibbs-White] is in.

It has been revealed that “It’s one thing to be nominated, but it’s another thing to perform. This also counts, especially Cole needs to step up to justify the nomination.”.

According to recent reports, “The minimum I can do is back my bosses. They have my full support on that.

“I’m grateful that I can talk about football because that’s my little bit of knowledge, not sports politics.”.

Industry observers note that “That’s the beauty of high-level sport, you can’t always win and it makes you feel alive. Not in a very nice way, still you feel that pain of these high-pressure moments.

“As soon as you enter knockout football, it’s a upcoming level of pressure.”.

Tuchel has now claimed that people say the 6-4 against France is “maybe one of their best experiences (watching football) ever”.

It has been revealed that again, not something anyone has remarked to me. Where is Tuchel finding these people?!

Tuchel on Alexander-Arnold: “He comes as a right back.” Sounds like he agrees with Mourinho that the Real Madrid player is not a midfielder.

Tuchel: “There was never a doubt in my mind that we would continue together and there was obviously never a doubt in their (the FA’s) mind.”.

Sources indicate that tuchel claims that 99.9 per cent of fans don’t talk about substitutions. He says they speak about the Mexico game and the Croatia game, their emotions and where they watched the matches.

Sorry, Thomas, that’s not my experience at all. Everyone I speak to indicates he blew the Argentina game. This sounds a bit deluded. According to Tuchel, I must speak to 0.01 per cent of England fans....

FA technical director John McDermott, who has taken a position at the back of the room to listen, had a little laugh when Tuchel joked that he got told off in his FA review for “my substitutions.”.

Tuchel indicates he felt the “full support from my bosses”.

Warning for Palmer: “It’s one thing to get your ticket back, but it’s another thing to keep it.”.

He’s expecting Palmer to step up and show him his Chelsea form.

“When you are a coach, you only win when you win...There’s not much sense torturing ourselves by looking back. I will not allow 30 minutes of the World Cup to determine how we view the World Cup.”.

In a recent development, tuchel states he has no regrets over not taking Palmer and Alexander-Arnold to the World Cup. He says he didn’t have a single sleepless night over his squad selection.

Tuchel claims the direction in sports is always forwards and never backwards. “The target is to win the home Euros, of course.”.

Recent findings suggest that tuchel notes his feelings on the World Cup are mixed. He thinks there are very positive things to take from the World Cup, but says it was also unfulfilled. He says it’s notable to recognise that England won a bronze medal, but says he acknowledges they did not push it over the line.

He notes the downside of having the belief they could go and win it is that it hurts even more that they did not.

Tuchel has stated the France third-place game “directs the narrative” of what’s coming for England.

Industry observers note that tuchel will be happy with this so far. Very gentle start from the broadcasters.

Recent findings suggest that no questions from the broadcasters about blowing the lead against Argentina and Tuchel’s opinion about the World Cup. Weird.

According to recent reports, ben White pulled out with an injury after being back to his best. It is unfortunately, a bit of a story for him. Josh King was very close and is on the radar.

Tuchel seems to be referring to notes as he speaks. He keeps looking down at a piece of paper he brought in with him.

“The door is always open through performance, behaviour and commitment.”.

“They had a good start to the season. Now it’s a new competition. Some positions have injuries. Palmer has his numbers back and a point to prove. Trent was never non-selectable and comes in as a right back.”.

Sources indicate that we will be hearing from Tuchel very soon. Lots to discuss but the Palmer and Alexander-Arnold call-ups and his World Cup reflections are at the top of the list.

Jason Steele’s inclusion is effectively a call-up. He was at the World Cup as a “fourth” goalkeeper for training – and going to country and western gigs in Kansas – but was not part of the official 26-man squad.

Sources indicate that the big ‘loser’ from the World Cup squad in being left out by Thomas Tuchel is Arsenal’s Noni Madueke. It is understood the place of his club team-mate Eberechi Eze was also in question, but the 28-year-old has been included, partly because of the unavailability of other players. Hopefully Thomas Tuchel will explain all later.

Thomas Tuchel has named his England squad for the first games of the 2026-27 season, as the Three Lions begin a latest Uefa Nations League campaign.

The head coach has selected a 27-man squad for the four-game window, which takes place between September 21 and October 6.

There’s a return to the Three Lions squad for a number of players following the start of the latest campaign with their clubs, with the likes of Cole Palmer, Dominic Calvert-Lewin, Lewis Hall, Rio Ngumoha, Jarrad Branthwaite, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Alex Scott all selected.

Eberechi Eze could be left out of the England squad announced this morning by Thomas Tuchel ahead of the forthcoming Nations League campaign. The Arsenal midfielder has made six appearances for his club so far this season but has only started two of those games and none in the Premier League.

#37557. Industry News: Zubimendi addresses tiredness and transfer talk

Industry News: Zubimendi addresses tiredness and transfer talk

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that good morning all, hope you’re well!
  • Martin was, as the story goes, a 4th-Century Roman soldier and is best known for sharing his cloak with a freezing beggar.
  • Recent findings suggest that fitting, then, that Martin Zubimendi should be linked with a move to Chelsea (and others).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that good morning all, hope you’re well! It’s St. Martin’s Day in Germany, a day I’d never heard of until I had a child over here. Kids will leave Kindergarten and chant as they walk through their neighbourhoods with lanterns this evening, as is tradition. Doesn’t sound creepy at all, does it?

St. Martin was, as the story goes, a 4th-Century Roman soldier and is best known for sharing his cloak with a freezing beggar.

Recent findings suggest that fitting, then, that Martin Zubimendi should be linked with a move to Chelsea (and others). It would be the saintly thing to do to share some of our midfield spoils with the desperate, downtrodden, shivering squad that Xabi Alonso has at his disposal. I hope we let them get absolutely glacial – Siberian, even, given their history – and keep our glorious cloak of midfielders all to ourselves.

The first rule of the international break is, of course, to ignore all transfer rumours. Club football goes away but there are still pages to fill, newspapers to sell, online traffic to amass, and something has to fill the void.

And, speaking to Marca, the midfielder has denied that he’s unhappy:.

I’m calm and happy with how I’m handling this situation. (Not playing) is something I’ve never experienced before, and I think you learn from these situations too.

I’m patient. When you’ve been playing a lot of minutes and your role changes to not playing as much, I’m able to see the positive side. I think everything passes, that just like last year the opposite happened to me and I played practically everything, this can change very quickly.

Asked about the toll that playing so much took on him last season – Zubimendi was the only Arsenal player to play in all 38 Premier League games, he started 34 of those and had the third most minutes in the squad, behind David Raya and Declan Rice, across all competitions – he admitted that that was a factor:.

Recent findings suggest that I don’t like to blame everything on my physical condition, but I definitely noticed it that year. It was a newly introduced year for me, with a lot of new stimuli. I played a huge number of minutes and, to be honest, I was tired. Then there were other things too, but one of them could very well have been my physical condition.

In a recent development, I spoke with Mikel at the beginning of the season. As he does with all the players, he explained the plan to me. He warned me that there were fresh signings and that there would be playing time for everyone. And here we are, fighting for it.

And he completely dismissed any suggestion that he is talking to other clubs, given those links to the Madrid sides and Chelsea:.

I haven’t wasted any energy on outside things. I’m busy enough trying to earn a place, get playing time, and fight to win this Premier League, which is looking so promising. I haven’t spent any energy on it, nor have I contacted anyone.

To be honest, I’m sometimes surprised by the press too. I understand that the winter transfer window is approaching and rumours can surface, but I think we need to be a bit more careful with what we publish. Ultimately, everyone has a team they play for, and we need to respect that. I’ve also read that I might be close (to a transfer), but not at all.

It has been revealed that still, I do think the case of Zubimendi is an interesting one. Having lost his place late last season, he returned late in the summer, and is yet to start a Premier League game in 2026-27 following the emergence of Myles Lewis-Skelly and the arrival of Bruno Guimaraes.

Here we have a player Arsenal desperately wanted and agreed a deal for a year ahead of signing him, would they really be looking to move him on again now that he’s spent what is essentially just a quarter of a season not as first choice? So much focus has been placed on building a squad that can sustain injuries or absences, and then we’d leave ourselves light again?

Maybe? You never can know how transfers pan out ahead of time, and things can change quickly in football but, as Zubimendi suggests, they can change quickly in the other direction again too. Did anyone, for instance, envisage Lewis-Skelly starting against Atletico Madrid just a week before it actually happened?

In a recent development, I do think his particular rise, and a stressful second half of the season, has clouded what we all thought of Zubimendi’s first half-season at Arsenal, and how much he contributed across the entire campaign. At this stage a year ago, we were two points worse off than we are now but still top of the league by six points, with more goals scored and fewer goals conceded than we are 10 games in this time around. He was a major part of that.

It has been revealed that he was a huge part of winning the title and reaching the Champions League final – he started 43 of our 53 games across those two competitions. He started every Champions League knockout game up until the semi-final second leg and played all of extra-time in the final.

And if he was suffering physically, there was no break in the summer, as he went off to the World Cup, Spain went all the way, and he was back on the pitch for Arsenal (having had no pre-season) in Cardiff as we won the Community Shield, less than a month on from the World Cup final.

It has been revealed that for all that, I can also see why someone would possibly want to make the case for moving on. Seeing a player not be used (Zubimendi has played in seven of our league games so far this season, by the way!) feels like an obvious place to upgrade, and we’ve been scarred before by letting players sit on the bench before then struggling to move them on for a fair fee.

According to recent reports, we’re also going to need to refresh the age of the team and especially the midfield before long. When you don’t just look at the players themselves but actually account for who is playing the minutes, we have the third-oldest squad in the league this season. The frontline will need new faces soon – that’s not news to anyone – in terms of age as well as quality, but the midfield will need it on the age front as well.

We’ve also given the fewest minutes in the league to players under the age of 23 (around 6%) by some distance. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it, but if you don’t get the balance right it will break in time.

According to recent reports, right now, though, this season, we’re likely to need our whole squad. We can’t be making it weaker. If one of Declan Rice – God forbid – or Bruno Guimaraes were to pick up a knock and miss a month, Zubimendi would suddenly be in line for a lot of football. Zubimendi who, again, was central to us winning the league last season.

It’s far too soon into the season to write his campaign off, especially when we saw how things changed so suddenly in that exact position back in May. Let’s see how things look when the summer rolls around, but there’s no need to rush into a decision.

Right then, have a great day all – and I’ll leave you with the gorgeous generosity of another St. Martin close to our hearts.

Galatasaray forward Victor Osimhen is allegedly 'flattered' by speculation linking him to Manchester United.

Mauricio Pochettino takes charge of his first Red Devils fixture on Sunday when his team face Liverpool at Anfield.

There is an argument that United need to enter the transfer market for a upcoming left-back and centre-back over any other position.

However, with Benjamin Sesko sidelined in the long term, consideration will be given to adding a fresh face to the attack.

According to The Sun, Osimhen would be interested in taking an opportunity to move to Old Trafford.

The report claims that the Nigeria international is 'flattered' by suggestions that United could make a fresh move for his signature.

Osimhen has been linked with a transfer to the Premier League in the past, only for his wage demands or asking price at Napoli to allegedly provide a stumbling block.

Nevertheless, it is noted that the 27-year-old still has ambitions to move to English football at some stage of his career.

As it stands, his contract at Galatasaray - which runs until the summer of 2029 - is likely to prevent any transfer from occurring in January.

That is seemingly partly a consequence of no release clause being present in his contract, while Galatasaray will not want to weaken their position in the Super Lig title race.

Ten goals and three assists have been contributed in his 11 appearances in Turkey's top flight and the Champions League this season.

Man United CEO Omar Berrada said in an interview with Sky Sports News this week that the club had been "disciplined" in the transfer market, and that is expected to remain the case.

Not only is Osimhen noted to be on a contract at Galatasaray in the region of £13m per year, his club would demand in excess of £50m for his signature as a bare minimum.

United are unlikely to be able to afford those terms at this time, particularly when it is apparent that other positions need strengthening.

#37554. Quantum resistance paradox of low-dimensional superfluids

Quantum resistance paradox of low-dimensional superfluids

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 50 min read (9958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~50 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that resistance in standard conductors decreases with increasing cross-section.
  • In a recent development, the Landau model provides a powerful framework for understanding many phases of matter through the lens of spontaneous symmetry breaking6,7.
  • In a recent development, for example, in a voltage-biased superconducting wire, the applied voltage continuously winds the superconducting phase, causing an increase of the phase gradient between the contacts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that resistance in standard conductors decreases with increasing cross-section. Yet, in low-dimensional superconductors and superfluids, residual resistance arises from topological fluctuations of the order parameter, manifesting as phase slips in one-dimensional (1D) and vortices in two-dimensional (2D) systems. How resistance and dissipation evolve as geometry interpolates between these regimes remains an open question. This evolution is masked in solid-state experiments by disorder, impurities and geometric imperfections1,2,3, and poses theoretical challenges due to competing dissipative processes and pronounced finite-size effects. Here, we use a defect-free unitary Fermi gas in a digitally programmable transport geometry to isolate geometric effects on superfluid dissipation and discover a paradox: in the crossover from one dimension to two dimensions, the resistance reaches a minimum. There, widening a channel increases its resistance. Narrower, quasi-1D channels show dissipation described by Langer–Ambegaokar–McCumber–Halperin theory of phase slips4. In this regime, varying the channel width yields the predicted exponential scaling of the activation factor over many orders of magnitude. Wider, quasi-2D channels show dissipation consistent with phase-slip events described by a finite-size vortex model5. The minimal dissipation in the dimensional crossover reflects a transition in the dominant dissipative mechanism, with both 1D and 2D events simultaneously suppressed. Our measurements suggest a route to minimizing dissipation in superconducting devices and provide a benchmark for theoretical efforts aimed at describing the dimensional crossover.

In a recent development, the Landau model provides a powerful framework for understanding many phases of matter through the lens of spontaneous symmetry breaking6,7. In superfluids and superconductors, this breaking manifests in the emergence of a macroscopic condensate that exhibits long-range phase coherence. This coherence is ultimately responsible for properties such as dissipationless transport8,9, the Josephson effect10, and in the case of superconductivity the Meissner effect11. Although relatively robust in bulk systems, in lower-dimensional systems, the enhanced effect of fluctuations—and in particular topological defects—can suppress this long-range phase coherence and govern superfluid transport4,12.

In a recent development, for example, in a voltage-biased superconducting wire, the applied voltage continuously winds the superconducting phase, causing an increase of the phase gradient between the contacts. The supercurrent, proportional to this gradient, would grow without bound unless intermittent phase fluctuations relax the accumulated gradient. By relaxing the gradient, the fluctuations dissipate energy, thereby causing a resistance3,13. The characteristics of the fluctuations and their corresponding resistance depend on the dimensionality of the setup as follows.

It has been revealed that in one-dimensional (1D) wires, discrete relaxation events known as phase slips dominate the dynamics. Microscopically, a phase slip occurs when the magnitude of the superconducting order parameter is transiently and locally suppressed over a healing length ξ. Where the amplitude vanishes, the phase is ill-defined, allowing for phase jumps of 2π. As the order parameter recovers, the wire returns to a state with a uniform amplitude but a reduced phase gradient4 (Fig. 1a, top row).

According to recent reports, a, Dissipation in a narrow, quasi-1D channel occurs because of phase slips, in which a depletion of the order parameter allows for a relaxation of the phase gradient and kinetic energy (top row). The corresponding phase (colour-coded) evolution of a phase slip in a narrow channel is plotted in the central row. In a wide, quasi-2D channel, dissipation is governed by vortex–antivortex pairs traversing the channel (bottom row). b, A transport channel of programmable width connects two superfluid reservoirs (blue). The channel is formed by two repulsive beams (green and orange), one of which is tunable by a DMD.

In two-dimensional (2D) geometries, such as thin films, dissipation instead arises from the nucleation and motion of topological defects known as vortices. A vortex is a point-like singularity of the phase around which the phase winds by 2π, with a small core in which the amplitude is suppressed. Driven by a current, vortices move across the film and dissipate energy. Each time a vortex traverses the sample, the phase difference between the contacts relaxes by 2π. Repeated vortex crossings generate a finite voltage and hence an effective resistance14,15 (Fig. 1a, bottom row). In intermediate, thin-strip geometries, both vortex flow and phase slips may contribute to dissipation.

Recent findings suggest that previous studies included experiments on superconducting rings16; Dayem-bridge nanowires17,18,19,20; Bose–Einstein condensates in dumbbell21,22, cylindrical23 or toroidal geometries24; optical lattices25,26; and fermionic Josephson junctions27,28,29. These previous studies have explored various facets of phase-slip and vortex physics, including direct imaging of vortices28,30,31,32, the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless phase transition33 and the recent observation of Shapiro steps in atomic Josephson junctions34,35. However, the experimental challenge of isolating and characterizing geometric or dimensional effects on dissipation remains unresolved.

With the rise of quantum simulation of devices based on highly controllable ultracold atomic gases36,37, it is now possible to shed new light on how these dissipative processes emerge in quantum systems.

In this work, we use ultracold, strongly interacting fermions in a two-terminal configuration to study nonlinear transport through a digitally programmable channel. The optically shaped channel can be reproducibly tuned from a quasi-1D to a quasi-2D geometry, providing a platform ideally suited for probing the influence of geometry on fluctuation-driven dissipation in the absence of defects or impurities.

In the narrow, 1D channel limit, we identify signatures of phase slips, in agreement with the Langer–Ambegaokar–McCumber–Halperin (LAMH) theory4,38,39. In particular, we observe the predicted exponential suppression of the LAMH activation factor over many orders of magnitude on widening the channel. For even larger widths, the system crosses over to a 2D regime in which dissipation is dominated by vortices, as indicated by the observed power-law dependence of the current–voltage characteristics predicted for vortex dynamics.

Beyond establishing these limiting behaviours, our measurements provide a direct window into the crossover between 1D and 2D transport, a regime in which analytical modelling is challenging. It is in this crossover that widening the channel paradoxically increases its resistance. More broadly, our results highlight the utility of ultracold atomic superfluids as a platform for quantum simulation of nonequilibrium transport.

We prepare a balanced mixture of the lowest and third-lowest hyperfine states of fermionic 6Li in the unitary regime. A total of 2N = 2.7 ± 0.1 × 105 atoms are cooled to T/TF = 0.144 ± 0.007, where N denotes the number of atom pairs, TF denotes the Fermi temperature, and the errors in both quantities denote the uncertainties due to shot-to-shot fluctuations. The temperature corresponds to T/TC ≈ 0.7, where TC ≈ 0.2TF denotes the critical temperature40. The atoms are confined in a cigar-shaped, harmonic trap with trapping frequencies (νx, νy, νz) = (222 ± 7, 28.1 ± 0.1, 195 ± 5) Hz.

As shown in Fig. 1a, a repulsive TEM0,1 beam, propagating in the x-direction, is aligned with the trap centre. It divides the atomic cloud into two reservoirs, separated by a quasi-2D transport region that is 51 ± 1 μm long and provides confinement of ν2D = 10.46 ± 0.09 kHz along z. Within the central 27 ± 0.5 μm of this plane, the atoms are further confined in the x-direction to a channel of variable width w. The channel is defined by a repulsive beam propagating along z, shaped by a digital micromirror device (DMD). It enables reproducible tunability of w from 0.9 ± 0.5 μm to 19.8 ± 0.5 μm, in which the uncertainty is dominated by and calculated from the resolution limit of our projection system (numerical aperture = 0.53, λ = 532 nm). Note that given the dimensions of our setup, we are not in the Josephson regime (see Methods, ‘No Josephson oscillations’). A third, attractive Gaussian beam (not shown) illuminates the transport channel and its connections to the reservoirs, locally increasing the degeneracy. A more detailed description of this effect as well as of the overall setup can be found in ref. 41.

At time t = 0, we prepare a relative atom-pair imbalance between the two reservoirs, ΔN/N = (Nl − Nr)/(Nl + Nr), where Nl,r denote the number of atom pairs in the left and right reservoirs. An initial imbalance of ΔN/N ≈ 0.1 relaxes through an approximately constant initial current, followed by damped oscillations of the imbalance. The discharge is distinctly non-exponential, indicating a nonlinear response. The damping, and in particular its dependence on the channel width w, carries information about the underlying microscopic mechanisms.

Recent findings suggest that the key data of our measurement series are shown in Fig. 2a. We record transport traces for w between 0.9 ± 0.5 μm and 19.8 ± 0.5 μm. As w increases, the magnitude of the initial current increases, which manifests in a steeper initial slope. Concurrently, both the oscillation frequency and amplitude grow. The frequency rises from just below 10 Hz to approximately 18 Hz (see also Extended Data Fig. 1). For the narrowest channel (w = 0.9 ± 0.5 μm), the oscillation amplitude is comparable to the noise floor and barely resolved. By contrast, for the widest channel (w = 19.8 ± 0.5 μm), the amplitude reaches ΔN/N ≈ 0.06.

a, Atom transport (imbalance ΔN/N as a function of time t) of a unitary Fermi gas through channels of increasing width demonstrates distinctively changing dissipation characteristics. The data are compared with fitted phase slip (LAMH) and vortex models. The models both describe the TNR in the circuit (b), capturing either phase slips or vortices. The LAMH model fits narrow channels, whereas the vortex model fits wide channels. The measurements for different channel widths are vertically offset for clarity. The statistical uncertainties of the measurements (typically four to five measurements per data point) are smaller than the marker size. c, A quality-of-fit \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis substantiates the change of the dominant model apparent in a.

Industry observers note that the damping exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on w. At longer transport times (for example, t = 0.3 s), the remaining oscillation amplitude reaches a maximum for intermediate channel widths (see also Fig. 4). These signals suggest distinct dissipative mechanisms in the narrow and wide channel limits, which we analyse quantitatively below.

Sources indicate that the general characteristics of the dynamics can be understood as arising from the interplay between the potential energy stored in the reservoirs, the kinetic energy inside the channel and the dissipative processes we want to investigate. To study these dissipative processes, we model our system with an equivalent RLC circuit shown in Fig. 2b. We first characterize the capacitance and inductance of the circuit to subsequently infer the dissipative (resistive) processes by fitting the dynamics of the circuit to the measurements. The capacitances, inductance and resistance in the circuit model correspond to the compressibility of the atomic reservoirs, the inertia of the atoms and the dissipative processes in the channel, respectively. We explore these elements in the following starting with the capacitors. As the model circuit features two capacitors in series, each with a capacitance C, the effective capacitance of the circuit is Ceff = C/2. The compressibility κeff of the gas allows to quantify this equivalent capacitance Ceff (potential energy per atom pair displaced from equilibrium) through \(\frac{1}{2}{(\Delta N/2)}^{2}/{\kappa }_{\mathrm{eff}}=\Delta {E}_{\mathrm{pot}}\equiv \frac{1}{2}{(\Delta N/2)}^{2}/{C}_{\mathrm{eff}}\). We measured the compressibility of our sample (Methods, ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’) to find hCeff = 15.8 ± 0.5 s, where h is Planck’s constant. Next we quantify the inductance. To do so, we assume all channels have box-like potentials. A charge-neutral atom-pair current I carries a kinetic energy Ekin that depends on w. We define the inductance of our systems using \({E}_{{\rm{kin}}}\equiv \frac{1}{2}L{I}^{2}.\) We developed a model that predicts a functional dependence.

(Methods, ‘Derivation of the inductance’). By analysing the oscillation frequencies observed in our measurements and noting that in a weakly damped circuit, the frequencies are given by \(\omega (w)\approx 1/\sqrt{L(w){C}_{\mathrm{eff}}}\), we find ℓc/h = 3.01 ± 0.03 × 10−5 μm s and Lres/h = 3.06 ± 0.04 × 10−6 s. Although the details are provided in the Supplementary Information, here we state that the first term in equation (1) captures the kinetic energy in the channel, whereas the second term accounts for the kinetic energy in the reservoirs.

Phase slips and vortices dissipate the kinetic energy of the current into heat. So, they effectively act as a topological nonlinear resistor (TNR). With L and C determined, the resistance R remains the sole unknown component in our circuit. Owing to the nature of phase slips, R is topological and nonlinear, meaning it depends not only on the geometry but also on the current.

Showing how R depends on geometry, in particular in relation to the length scale given by ξ ≈ 1.2 μm (Methods, ‘Estimate of ξ’), reveals the nature of the underlying dissipative processes. To do so, we fit the width-dependent resistance R(w) in the equations of motion of an RLC circuit (derived in Methods, ‘RLC circuit modelling and fitting’).

Recent findings suggest that for narrow, quasi-1D channels (w ≱ 2ξ), we expect the system to be in the phase slip regime. The LAMH model predicts4.

defined using R = V/I, where R0 is the characteristic resistance, w0 is the characteristic width, and I0 = 2kBT/h, where kB is the Boltzmann’s constant and T is the temperature. The exponential suppression of R with w reflects the thermally activated phase-slip rate scaling with \(\varGamma \propto \exp (-\Delta F/({k}_{{\rm{B}}}T))\) (ref. 18), where the free energy barrier for phase slips is ΔF ∝ w. The sinh(I/I0) term can intuitively be understood as follows: at small |I/I0| ≪ 1, phase slips occur in both directions with roughly equal probability; as the bias increases slightly, phase slips that relax the current become more probable. For large |I/I0| ≫ 1, sinh(I/I0) ≈ exp(I/I0)/2. reflecting the local destabilization of the superfluid and the resulting exponential increase in the phase-slip probability.

In a recent development, using our predetermined C and L(w), we determine R0 and w0 by fitting them simultaneously to the measurements of our four narrowest channels (Methods, ‘RLC circuit modelling and fitting’). Assuming that the LAMH model can be used to describe our system, a simultaneous fit to multiple channel widths provides a robust extraction of the model parameters but enforces the predicted exponential suppression of RLAMH with w. We find R0/h = 102.3±0.2 and w0 = 49.7(6) nm, where the errors denote the uncertainties of the fit. The resulting fits (shown in Fig. 2a) largely capture the dynamics for channels with a width up to w = 2.5 μm. This is quantified by \(\mathrm{NRMSE}\,=\) \(\sqrt{{\sum }_{i}{({m}_{i}-{f}_{i})}^{2}/N}/({m}_{\max }-{m}_{\min }) < 0.06\), where mi and fi denote the measured and fitted imbalances, respectively, and mmax − mmin is the measured signal range. However, the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis \(({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\lesssim 9)\) shown in Fig. 2c suggests additional systematic effects beyond the very small statistical uncertainties of the measurements (typically on the level of 0.004). These systematic effects could originate from the approximation of modelling the channel with a box-like potential or the attractive beam illuminating the channel locally increasing the temperature. Outside the validity range of the model, the quality of the fits degrades noticeably, failing to capture the phase of the oscillations and underestimating their damping.

According to recent reports, in a second step, we validate the choice of the LAMH model by fitting RLAMH(w) to each curve individually. In contrast to the simultaneous fit, these individual fits do not enforce the predicted scaling RLAMH(w) and therefore provide an independent test of whether the scaling is present in the data. Within the validity regime of the model, the individual fits reproduce the predicted exponential scaling over many orders of magnitude, as shown in Fig. 3a.

Industry observers note that a, The fitted phase-slip resistance RLAMH(w), for narrow channels, demonstrates the exponential suppression with width, as predicted by LAMH theory. b, The fitted vortex resistivity ρv(w), for wide channels, shows the predicted power law. Inside the crossover region (2–4ξ), that is, outside the validity range of the models, both scalings break down (Methods, ‘Breakdown of scaling laws’). Note that a and b display different quantities (resistance compared with resistivity) characterizing different regimes (1D compared with 2D) and are therefore not intended to be compared across the dimensional crossover. The error bars represent the error of the fit.

This is the first main finding of this paper. Compared with RLAMH(w), the total resistance R(I, w) apparent in the measurements (Fig. 2a) varies much less. As we initialize a fixed potential bias in our system, the exponential geometric suppression (R ∝ exp(−w/w0)) approximately cancels the current-induced exponential enhancement (R ∝ sinh(I/I0) ≈ exp(I/I0)/2). This allows RLAMH to be inferred over a wide range—more than 10 decades—while only exploring a relatively modest dynamic range of R. Importantly, the observed scaling of RLAMH(w) is contained within the data itself and is not just an artefact of the choice of the model. This becomes evident when the model is applied outside its validity regime, where the scaling breaks down immediately (Methods, ‘Breakdown of scaling laws’).

Recent findings suggest that in quasi-2D channels (w ≳ 4ξ), phase slips become energetically unfavourable, as their activation energy increases exponentially with w. Instead, dissipation is expected to be governed by vortex flow. Owing to the vortices, we expect to see a power-law dependence in the pair-current density J:.

where J0 = I0/ξ. A derivation, building on the results of ref. 5, is provided in the Methods, ‘Vortices in a finite width’. By fitting α and \({\widetilde{R}}_{0}\) simultaneously to the data of our four widest channels (Methods, ‘RLC circuit modelling and fitting’), we find \(\alpha =1.98\pm 0.04,{\mathop{R}\limits^{ \sim }}_{0}/h=1{0}^{-4.79\pm 0.07}\). As apparent from Fig. 2a, this model captures the dynamics for channels in the 2D regime (NRMSE ≱ 0.06). In these cases, \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\lesssim 4\). Note that the vortex model does not contain an explicit temperature dependence, and for wide channels, the box-potential approximation is safer compared with narrow channels. Apart from these statistical tests, we validate our model by fixing α to its global fit value but fitting ρv to each individual curve. Within the validity range of the model, these individual fits agree with the predicted power-law ρv ∝ wα−1 (Fig. 3b). This scaling is the second main finding of the paper. The scaling breaks down outside the validity regime of the model (Methods, ‘Breakdown of scaling laws’), providing evidence that the observed scaling is a feature of the data, not a mere artefact of the enforced power law R ∝ Jα−1. When approaching the dimensional crossover w ≱ 4ξ, while still largely capturing the dynamics, the model begins to slightly but systematically underestimate the amplitude of the oscillations at long times. Presumably, because the approximation of sufficiently large w used in the derivation of R(J) ceases to hold (Methods, ‘Vortices in a finite width’). The eventual breakdown of the vortex model at w ≈ 4ξ marks the end of the 2D regime: the vortex model should be valid only when vortex–antivortex pairs are available as excitations. As each vortex has a radius of ξ, such an excitation requires w ≳ 4ξ. This leaves a gap between the validity ranges of the phase slip and the vortex model, in which neither model provides a microscopically satisfactory description. In this gap, there is a dimensional crossover, in which both phase slips and vortices compete.

It has been revealed that the underdamped oscillations allow us to characterize dissipation in our system using only a few basic assumptions, while staying agnostic to the dissipation mechanism. This is particularly useful to analyse the dimensional crossover, in which neither the phase-slip nor the vortex model provide a satisfactory microscopical description. We split the total energy Etot into a potential (capacitive) energy EC and a kinetic (inductive) energy EL. We assume Etot = EC(ΔN) + EL(I, w) with EC ∝ ΔN2 and EL(I = 0, w) = 0. For each channel width w, we extract the times ti,w at which ΔN(t = ti, w) reaches an extremum and thus I ≈ 0. There, the system has minimal inductive energy (EL ≈ 0) and maximal capacitive energy. The fraction of the initial energy remaining in the system is then given by.

Sources indicate that the remaining energy as a function of time and channel width is shown in Fig. 4. The plot is obtained by cubic interpolation between the measured points, performed linearly in time and logarithmically in width.

The remaining energy in the oscillator paradoxically varies non-monotonically as a function of the channel width w. For a given time after the initial decay, the maximum appears in the crossover region, near w = 4 μm ≈ 3ξ, in which phase slips and vortices are suppressed but competing. The crosses mark the measurement points (typically four to five measurements per cross) between which we interpolate. We estimate the individual data points to have a typical positive bias of 0.5% and a statistical uncertainty smaller than 2% (Methods, ‘Error estimation’).

For a fixed width, the energy decays over time, reflecting dissipation. At any given time t > 0.15 s, Et(w)/E0 varies non-monotonically with the channel width, exhibiting a clear maximum near w ≈ 3ξ, corresponding to a minimal effective resistance. We call this deviation from the expected monotonicity the ‘quantum resistance paradox’ and consider it the third and last main finding of this paper. Note that the activation energy for phase slips increases exponentially with channel width, whereas vortex–antivortex pairs require sufficiently wide channels to form. The observed non-monotonicity thus suggests a transition in the underlying dissipation mechanism and a crossover from 1D to 2D physics.

We have investigated atom transport between two bulk superfluids through channels across different dimensional regimes and observed distinct behaviours. In narrow, quasi-1D channels, our data are in agreement with those of the LAMH model. We infer the geometric suppression of the phase slips by many orders of magnitude, providing the first experimental confirmation of the predicted geometric scaling. For wide, quasi-2D channels, dissipation is captured by a vortex flow model. The borders of the 1D and 2D regimes appear close to the theoretically expected length scale. A measurement of energy decay, agnostic to microscopic details, provides further evidence for a transition in the dissipation mechanism for channels of intermediate width, which paradoxically exhibit the least energy loss. These findings not only suggest routes for optimizing energy transport in mesoscopic devices but also provide a benchmark for theoretical efforts to describe the delicate phase-slip and vortex-flow mechanisms in the dimensional crossover in superfluids and superconductors42,43,44.

Our setup is analogous to an RLC circuit with the mapping presented in Extended Data Table 1.

The procedures for determining the capacitance C and the inductance L are described in sections ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’ and ‘Derivation of the inductance’. Here, we derive the governing equations and provide additional details on the fitting procedure used to determine R, as presented in the main text.

Recent findings suggest that the total number of atoms in each reservoir is measured directly using absorption images of both hyperfine states (|1⟩ and |3⟩), taken in rapid succession. To determine the total number of pairs in each reservoir Nl,r, we use both measurements, as this reduces statistical uncertainty. Specifically, \({N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}}}=({N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}};|1\rangle }+{N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}};|3\rangle })/2\), where \({N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}};|i\rangle }\) denotes the number of atoms in the left and right reservoirs in state |i⟩. However, the second image (state |3⟩) reveals a cloud that has absorbed some energy from the first imaging pulse and is therefore slightly distorted. To avoid systematic effects from this distortion on C and T, we use only the image of the lowest hyperfine state (|1⟩) to extract the compressibility and temperature of the cloud, assuming these are identical for both states. We verified that our preparation is equivalent for both states by inverting the imaging sequence. We describe our system in terms of pairs and report C, L and R for pairs and pair currents, respectively.

Experimentally, transport is initiated by ramping down a blue-detuned beam that blocks the channel. A sudden quench of this beam slightly perturbs the reservoirs, so we instead ramp it down over 10 ms. This introduces an unknown initial condition I(t = 0). For each curve, we fit I(t = 0) ∈ [0, Iavg], where Iavg is the average current during the initial decay (before oscillations). To avoid giving undue weight to the first measured point, we fit ΔNfit(t = 0) ∈ [0.8, 1.2] ⋅ ΔNmeasured(t = 0). These bounds are necessary to prevent the models from ignoring the initial decay outside their validity regime. In particular, this is the case for the LAMH model when fitting data of wide channels, where only a few points represent the initial dynamics.

For numerical stability, R0 and \({\widetilde{R}}_{0}\) are fitted on a logarithmic scale, whereas α and w0 are fitted linearly.

Recent findings suggest that finally, we discuss the fitting weights. Each configuration (t, w) has five measurements. Points with preparation errors (low atom number) are excluded, typically leaving four to five measurements per point and occasionally three. The experimental standard deviation is calculated for each configuration individually. We assume that for a given w, the uncertainty is independent of t. To prevent the fit from being dominated by points with unrealistically small uncertainties, both the fitting and the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) calculations replace individual error bars with the median error bar of all the data sharing w.

Sources indicate that the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis shown in Fig. 2c is performed as follows. The uncertainty of the measured points is assumed to be identical for all points belonging to a specific channel width. For each channel width, the model is fitted, either with 2.5 effective degrees of freedom (R0, w0, ΔN0, I0 or \({\widetilde{R}}_{0},\alpha ,\Delta {N}_{0},{I}_{0}\)), where the first two parameters are shared among four channels (2/4 = 0.5) if the channel participates in the global fit of the respective model, or two degrees of freedom (ΔN0, I0) otherwise. The reduced chi-squared is then calculated using \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}=\frac{1}{n-m}\sum \frac{{({m}_{i}-{f}_{i})}^{2}}{{\sigma }^{2}}\), where mi are the measured values, fi the corresponding values fitted by the model, σ the uncertainty shared by all measurement points of a specific width, n the number of measured points and m = 2.5 or m = 2 the number of effectively fitted degrees of freedom.

According to recent reports, we discuss how the fitted models are affected by the various sources of systematic uncertainty. Specifically, we investigate how systematic uncertainties in the capacitance C, the channel width w and the temperature T affect the quality of the model fits and the inferred parameters RLAMH and α.

Assume that the true physical capacitance \(\widetilde{C}\) differs from the calculated value (see section ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’) by a factor γ, such that \(C=\gamma \widetilde{C}\). In our analysis, the effective inductance L is determined (see section ‘Derivation of the inductance’) before fitting the resistance by analysing the underdamped, multi-period oscillations of the system. Owing to the observation of multiple periods, the frequency can be measured with good accuracy and precision. A systematic shift γ ≠ 1 would therefore result in an inverse scaling of the extracted inductance curve, \(L\approx \widetilde{L}/\gamma \), where \(\widetilde{L}\) represents the true physical inductance. Inspecting the underlying equation of motion of the circuit (equation (2)) highlights that the extracted resistance scales identically with this factor (R ∝ 1/γ). This uniform rescaling by 1/α can be absorbed in the prefactor R0 or \({\widetilde{R}}_{0}\), leaving the quality of the fits, scalings, the inferred dynamic ranges and the geometric suppression constant w0 entirely unaffected.

Sources indicate that the geometric potential landscape is projected onto the atoms using a DMD. Although physical pixel spacing and optical demagnification ratio are known accurately, the primary source of spatial uncertainty stems from the finite resolution of the imaging optics. The finite resolution effectively blurs the repulsive potential walls of the channel. Consequently, having to choose where to define the sharp boundaries of the model (spaced by w) within this blurred profile introduces a systematic uncertainty Δw.

According to recent reports, importantly, this geometric uncertainty of roughly 0.5 μm is expected to be shared across all channel configurations and does not affect each channel independently of the others. For channels in the 1D regime, the initial discharge through the narrowest channels is characterized by an extended period of nearly constant current in which inertial forces are negligible (∣L dI/dt∣ ≪ |RI|). In this regime, the system behaves predominantly as a nonlinear RC circuit, approximately decoupling the resistance fit from the precise value of L. Then, a uniform translation of w by Δw alters the resistances by a constant factor. For the LAMH model, \(R(w+\Delta w)\propto \exp (-\Delta w/{w}_{0})\). Similarly to the capacitance error, this effect is entirely absorbed by a re-normalization of the global prefactor R0, preserving both the dynamic range of RLAMH and its slope set by w0. The relatively high value of \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) for the LAMH model might be caused by the experiment that violates the assumption of box-like channel potentials. For the channels in the 2D regime, Δw/w ≪ 1, so we expect systematic effects caused by Δw ≠ 0 to be small and the approximation of modelling the channels as box-like to be safe.

Although we calibrated our measurements with the thermodynamic reference point of Bose–Einstein condensation, our measured atom-pair numbers and temperatures (see sections ‘High-saturation imaging’ and ‘Thermodynamic state extraction by 2D equation of state fitting’) might be subject to systematic errors. An error in the inferred pair-number \(N=\gamma \widetilde{N}\), where N is the inferred particle number and \(\widetilde{N}\) is the physical particle number, would force a corresponding shift in C, thereby rescaling L and R as discussed above. Moreover, it would rescale I. As the current enters the expression for the resistance in the vortex model only in the form of a power law, it would merely shift \(\widetilde{R}\) by a constant factor γ−α. Again, this constant factor would affect neither α, nor the quality of the vortex-model fits, nor the quality of its scaling law. As the vortex model does not contain an explicit temperature dependence, it is unaffected by potential systematic effects in T. For the LAMH model, the situation is different. The temperature enters the model explicitly through I0 = 2kBT/h. Variations in both N and T ultimately tie into the ratio I/I0. Because this ratio controls the degree of nonlinearity of the circuit, we can model their combined systematic impact by analysing variations in I0 alone.

Industry observers note that the initial discharge of the narrowest channels is distinctly nonlinear (implying I ≫ I0), whereas the subsequent oscillations are approximately sinusoidal (implying I ≱ I0). Consequently, the ratio I/I0 is constrained by the geometric profile of the relaxation curves. However, systematic effects that affect the ratio I/I0 do also affect the quality of fit and the dynamic range of RLAMH. In general, if I/I0 is lowered (by decreasing I or increasing T), the circuit is less nonlinear and the dynamic range of RLAMH decreases, whereas an increase in the ratio has the opposite effect. Although the parameter I0 is constrained in the LAMH model, we performed additional fittings, where I0 was a global fit parameter, to effectively account for potential systematic errors in I or T. The best fits are achieved with I0,fit = 3.50(1)I0, reducing \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) averaged over the five narrowest channels, by more than a factor of 2. A possible cause for this could be that the attractive Gaussian beam illuminating the channel locally heats the channel, thereby increasing I0. Note that this beam also increases the local degeneracy such that we would still expect the channel to be deeply degenerate. Although in the case of fitted I0, the dynamic range of RLAMH is reduced, it continues to span more than four orders of magnitude. The values are still in good agreement with the predicted exponential scaling.

It has been revealed that for all channel widths except the narrowest one, we observe underdamped, long-lived oscillations. As these oscillations remain underdamped, the influence of the nonlinear resistance on the oscillation frequency is expected to be small. To extract the inductance of the channel for each width (except the narrowest one), we exclude the initial transient dynamics up to the first, global minimum occurring at a time t = t1,w. The remaining data are fitted with a damped sinusoidal function \({f}_{w}(t)={A}_{w}\exp (-(t-{t}_{1,w})/{\tau }_{w})\sin ({\omega }_{w}t+{\phi }_{{\rm{w}}})+\Delta {N}_{w,\mathrm{offset}},\) where Aw, τw, ωw, ϕw, and ΔNw,offset are fitting parameters. Small offsets |ΔNw,offset| < 0.018 account for potential alignment errors that cause the oscillations to centre around slightly nonzero values. Using the inferred effective capacitance Ceff of our circuit (see section ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’), we determine the total inductance for a given channel width as \({L}_{w}=1/(({\omega }_{w}^{2}+{\tau }_{w}^{-2}){C}_{\mathrm{eff}})\approx 1/({\omega }_{w}^{2}C),\) where the approximation is equivalent to the result for an undamped LC circuit and holds for weakly damped circuits. Although the quantitative difference in our case is minute, we do include the τ-term capturing the effect of the resistance lowering the oscillation frequency of the RLC circuit. Note that for the wide channels in particular, fitting a damped sine to the oscillatory data is a pragmatic choice that allows for an approximation of the inductance, the signature of which is primarily contained in the frequency of the oscillation. Over extended periods of time, however, the damped sine and the dynamics of the vortex model would appear different, as the latter does not feature an exponentially decaying amplitude. This kinetic inductance Lw quantifies the kinetic energy associated with a given pair current I. Although the main contribution arises from the transport channel itself, there is also a residual contribution because of particle motion in the adjoining 2D and 3D regions, whose geometries are independent of the channel width. We therefore write \(L(w)={L}_{\mathrm{channel}}(w)+{L}_{\mathrm{res}}\). Assuming a constant particle density inside the channel, the mass of particles in the transport channel (M) scales with its width, M ∝ w. For a given current, the corresponding particle velocity in the channel thus scales inversely, \({v}_{\mathrm{channel}}\propto \frac{1}{w}\). Consequently, the kinetic energy associated with a fixed I scales as \({E}_{\mathrm{kin}}=M{v}_{\mathrm{channel}}^{2}/2\propto w{(1/w)}^{2}=1/w\), implying that Lchannel(w) ∝ 1/w. According to recent reports, in a previous, comparable experimental setting, we estimated the atoms traversing a region of length d ≈ 3 μm in a time t ≈ 330 μs, resulting in an estimated atomic velocity of v ≈ 9 mm s−1 (ref. 48). As our channel is practically defect free, we assume that the atomic velocity is close to the critical velocity vc. So we estimate 4ξ ≈ 4ħ/(mvc) ≈ 5 μm (ref. 49).

Sources indicate that given the method with which we extract the energy ratio, two main sources of error are to be considered. The first one is the statistical noise of the measurement points. This directly translates into an uncertainty of the inferred energy ratio but also causes a systematic bias towards higher values, as only the extrema of the signals are considered. The second contribution comes from the finite sampling rate of the oscillations. This causes an uncertainty and a bias towards lower values, as the measured points do not sample the peaks exactly. To quantitatively assess their influence for all our measurements, we performed Monte Carlo simulations. Specifically, we sampled sinusoidal signals with the frequencies, amplitudes and dampings observed in the signals used for Fig. 4. We sampled these artificial signals with the sampling rates and statistical noise that occurred in the physical experiment. This simulation yielded the following insight: For the data presented in Fig. 4, the inferred energies have a typical positive bias of 0.5% and a standard deviation smaller than 2%.

According to recent reports, although several studies have reported on Josephson oscillations with seemingly similar measurements in comparable settings27,28,29, our system operates far outside the Josephson regime. The Josephson effect requires the junction length to be much shorter than the superconducting coherence length, which for our system is close to the healing length4,12. In our case, the channel length ℓ = 27 μm is much larger than the estimated healing length ξ ≈ 1.2 μm (Methods, ‘Estimate of ξ’). Moreover, we observe neither a well-defined current-phase relation nor an oscillation amplitude consistent with the Josephson relation. The former statement is based on time-of-flight measurements of the relative phase of the two reservoirs with the same preparation performed in a slightly different geometry. Although for the data shown in this manuscript, we always observe the same initial dynamics (up to small noise), these additional measurements confirm that the prepared phase between the two reservoirs is not controlled, sampling values between 0 and 2π from a flat distribution. We therefore conclude that the oscillatory signal observed in our experiment cannot be attributed to JO.

Sources indicate that extended Data Fig. 2 provides additional data related to Fig. 3. The theoretical motivation and the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis presented in Fig. 2 already justify the choice of models. The data shown here complements that analysis by demonstrating that the scaling laws reported in Fig. 3 are not numerical artefacts and are not imposed by the fitting procedure.

In a recent development, for both the LAMH and vortex models, the predicted scalings break down outside their respective ranges of validity. This behaviour indicates that the observed scaling is not a numerical consequence of the fitting procedure and is not artificially enforced by the functional form of the models.

The saturation of the LAMH-inferred resistance at large widths does not seem to be due to limited fitting precision, fitting boundaries or lack of convergence. Instead, it reflects a transition from the strong exponential width dependence characteristic of the LAMH model to a much weaker dependence, as predicted by the vortex model.

For the vortex model, the trend reverses in the crossover regime, showing a clear deviation from the scaling expected by that model.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alphadjo Cisse has definitely been the breakout player of the season so far and Ruben Amorim has no intention of dialling down his presence in attack.
  • Milan had a very clear plan when they headed into the current season: Goncalo Ramos would be the main man in attack.
  • Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alphadjo Cisse has definitely been the breakout player of the season so far and Ruben Amorim has no intention of dialling down his presence in attack.

Milan had a very clear plan when they headed into the current season: Goncalo Ramos would be the main man in attack. Instead, however, it’s the underdog Cisse who has been running the show, while the Portuguese striker has been at the bottom in terms of output.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

As highlighted by Gazzetta dello Sport this morning (see image below), that’s why there cannot be – and likely won’t be – a Milan without Cisse in attack. Ruben Amorim now wants to build the attack around him, as opposed to introducing him every now and then.

According to recent reports, the most recent clash, the 2-1 win against Genoa, was a good example of this. Amorim went for a bold formation with Cisse, Ramos, Christian Pulisic, Diego Moreira, Luka Modric and Adrien Rabiot together. A team with a lot of quality and an attacking-minded style.

It was a shape that reminded us of 2009-10, when Milan were guided by another foreign coach: Leonardo. He chose a very attacking-minded side with four attackers and two midfielders, which is something that Amorim almost replicated.

Modric and Rabiot in front of the defence (Pirlo and Ambrosini then) and the fantasy project with Pulisic, Moreira, Cisse, and Ramos, comparable to the Ronaldinho, Pato, Seedorf, and Borriello of the old days.

Despite this, the goals were scored after two mistakes by Genoa (even if Milan’s pressing helped), so the goal is to repeat the experiment against Frosinone and to increase its effectiveness, the experiment should be repeated tomorrow.

Recent findings suggest that in that sense, Cisse will be notable as he’s the top scorer: three goals in Europa League and five in Serie A. He has scored with both feet and his head, demonstrating a combination of talent and an eye for goal: characteristics that are very important for a team like Milan.

The average also speaks for itself: eight goals spread across 658 minutes means he scores a goal every 82 minutes. Best of all, his versatility means that he can play as an attacking midfielder, a left-winger, and even as a centre-forward.

At just 20 years and 17 days old, thanks to the fifth goal in his ninth Serie A appearance, Cisse became the second-youngest player to reach the milestone in the first ten games with Milan, at least since 1994-95. Only Pato did it younger, at 18 years and 181 days.

Furthermore, he’s one of only three players born after 2006 (top five leagues) to have scored eight or more goals in all competitions, along with Lamine Yamal (13) and Paris Brunner, who also scored eight.

As the pink newspaper concludes, Ramos has also produced eye-catching numbers, but in this case in a negative sense: 1,191 minutes on the pitch, three goals scored, meaning one goal scored every 398 minutes.

#37552. The virtues of patience

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1317 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arseblog ↗ Open Full Page

The virtues of patience

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1317 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was freezing and wet at the Emirates.
  • Sources indicate that this was supposed to be fun.
  • Recent findings suggest that willian was grotesquely slow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let’s take a journey back in time.

It’s 13 December 2020. Arsenal versus Burnley.

It was freezing and wet at the Emirates. Only 2,000 fans had been allowed in because of Covid, and my mum, my dad, my mate Ben and I made up four of them. We were socially distanced and wearing masks. My glasses kept steaming up.

Sources indicate that this was supposed to be fun. Watching my team.

Recent findings suggest that willian was grotesquely slow. Alex Lacazette was profligate. Rob Holding was bald. Very bald. And Granit Xhaka was angry. So angry, in fact, that in the second half he put his hands around the throat of some opposition goon and, after a VAR review, got himself sent off. There were boos. As many as 2,000 people could muster, anyway.

Industry observers note that then our captain, Pierre Emerick-Aubameyang, headed a corner into his own net. You couldn’t make it up. Except you could. It was the only goal of the game.

Industry observers note that by then the steam fogging up my specs might as well have been coming out of my ears. In his player ratings, Andrew M called Xhaka the ‘King of the Idiots’ and described the match and the result as ‘utterly shit’. Which was fair.

It was our seventh defeat in 10 league games and our fourth in a row at home, something that hadn’t happened since 1953. We were 15th, five points above the relegation zone.

In a recent development, and who was top? Sp*rs. Managed by everyone’s favourite sociopath, Jose Mourinho. Having beaten us in the North London derby the week before, they couldn’t stop gloating.

I’d bought into the Arteta project hook, line and sinker. I still wanted him to be the right man for the job. I was just finding it harder to explain why I thought he was. The FA Cup win had been four months earlier. It felt like years.

The tree, to paraphrase our manager, was shaking.

It had been shaking for a good two and a half years by then. The soggy bottom of the Arsene Wenger era had left its scars. Those two 3-0 defeats to City in the space of a week still make me wince. Then came the hope that Unai Emery might get us back on track. By the time we’d seen how that played out, I’d got into the habit of talking myself down whenever things looked up. Maybe we’ll get better. Give it time.

It has been revealed that the trouble with rock bottom is you never know if there’s another floor below it. Was Burnley ours? I’m still writing about it six years later, so it was probably mine. There were games against Southampton and Everton before Christmas, and I can barely remember either of them.

Then came Boxing Day and a visit from Frank Lampard’s Chelsea. Is it reductive to say that was the day everything changed for Mikel Arteta’s Arsenal? Probably. But my word, watching Bukayo Saka, Emile Smith Rowe and Gabriel Martinelli tear about the place was the fix this addict needed. We went on an unbeaten run after that. Seven whole games! And for the first time in weeks, I was looking forward to what came next.

It has been revealed that and here we are in November 2026. Reigning champions of England. Top of the league again. Five points clear. Odds-on favourites to retain the title after 10 games. Sure, throwing hundreds of millions of American dollars at the problem helped. But if there’s a lesson in all this, it’s that hard work and patience pay off.

Which is why I’m using today’s blog to appeal directly to Sir Jim Ratcliffe to give Michael Carrick a stay of execution.

Recent findings suggest that come on, man, you’re probably still paying off Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim, maybe even Ralf Rangnick. Do you really want to go back to the drawing board all over again? Carrick is the man for the Manchester United hot seat. Just look at the way he wore a poppy-embroidered armband as well as a poppy badge at the weekend. The man doesn’t do half measures. He’s a two-scoops guy. Surely that’s something you, a multibillionaire British-born petrochemicals tycoon who lives in Monaco, can get on board with?

I know Mauricio Pochettino might be tempting. He’s got floppy hair, a tan and, despite the Sp*rsy stench, has come to resemble a rather huggable teddy bear. But think it through, Jim. What if he comes in and everybody perks up? It’s much harder to make job cuts and to force out season ticket holders when people are enjoying themselves. Best get through that process first while Michael turns the oil tanker round. It’s not far off, promise, you’re on a two-game unbeaten streak!

Anyway, what would sacking Carrick say about patience? Look at Arteta. There were people who wanted him gone after Burnley and, as you’ve just read, I was close to joining them. Imagine if the club had listened to me. All those years of work, all that progress, all the joy I’ve had watching Arsenal lately. We could have thrown it all away because a man in a damp mask couldn’t see out of his glasses.

Industry observers note that so give Carrick time. Give him January. Give him a full pre-season. And if things still haven’t picked up by this time next year, ask yourself whether one full pre-season, and £100 million on Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos, was ever really enough.

I can only speak for myself, Jim, but I haven’t looked forward to watching Manchester United this much in years.

Right, let’s see if that works….

The Interlull kicks into gear tonight. David Raya, Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi are in action for Spain against Czechia, Riccardo Calafiori’s Italy take on France, and England face Croatia at Wembley.

Ezri Konsa and Myles Lewis-Skelly will both miss out at Wembley. Konsa is working on his fitness but will be available to face Spain on Sunday, while our Hale Ender is suspended after picking up two bookings in the Nations League.

Elsewhere, ahead of Sweden’s game against Bosnia and Herzegovina, Viktor Gyokeres has been speaking to the press. Like Martin Zubimendi, he indicates he’s happy at Arsenal.

“I want to,” he said, when asked if he’s keen to stay at the Emirates.

“It feels good when I’ve played. We’ve won most of the games. It was a tough loss in the cup (against Fleetwood). Otherwise it’s felt good for myself and the team, states the forward. I’ve been doing well lately when I’ve been playing. Right now it feels good.

“The communication with (Mikel) Arteta is good. We talk about football and how we should play. Before a match, if I’m going to start, we talk about the opponents and what I should think about.”.

He was also asked whether the criticism he gets bothers him.

“Sometimes it might get to me, but overall not so much. If I score goals and assists in the Champions League, I couldn’t care less what they say. It’s nice to do those kinds of performances. To deliver for myself and for the team. That’s where the focus lies.”.

To be fair, I’ve not seen any serious chatter about selling Viktor in January. Whatever you think of him as a player, it would be a strange move unless we’re planning to spend serious money on the attack. And even then it would feel like an unnecessary risk given Kai isn’t exactly pulling up trees and new faces will need an adaptation period.

If he’s happy keeping his head down and doing his bit for the team, I’d keep him around until the summer and reassess then.

Ok. I’m going to leave it there for today. All eyes on Old Trafford, I guess.

#37551. Harry Kane injury could force Bayern Munich into £44m transfer dilemma amid Arsenal, Man United interest
